newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals - Japan aluminium premiums seen higher.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Japan aluminium premiums seen higher.

text.p: Japanese aluminium premiums, a benchmark for northeast Asia, are set to climb in the third quarter as bullish suppliers have the upper hand in talks that started this week, traders said on Wednesday.

"The third-quarter premiums are likely to be set around $85 to $90 (per tonne). They might end up as high as $95," said a trader at a major Japanese trading house. "Global demand for the metal is very strong."
Currently Japanese traders, large end-users and foreign aluminium producers are negotiating the metal's premiums in term contracts for deliveries in the July-September quarter.

Traders said the premiums, expected to be decided early next week, were likely to be set above $85 despite a consensus that Japanese demand would decline in the third quarter after a surge ahead of a sales tax increase in April.
Initially, traders hoped that premiums would decline from $82 in the April-June quarter, possibly below $80, as domestic premiums still stood at $75 to $80.

"Suppliers are bullish. I don't know what to do if they manage to push up the premiums very much," said another trader. "We won't see a rise in demand in the second half. We can expect only a dip following the tax hike."

Traders said the metal's premiums in spot trade have remained high at around $85/$90, reflecting a strong worldwide appetite for the metal that is evident in low warehouse stocks in London and firm U.S. Midwest premiums.
Traders said aluminium stocks in Yokohama also remained below 180,000 tonnes, well under usual levels above 200,000 tonnes, partly because high premiums elsewhere attracted metal away from Japan.

In the zinc market, premiums eased slightly as China was eager to expand exports to cash in on high LME zinc prices, although the Japanese market was still digesting heavy imports under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) scheme earlier this year.

"I wouldn't be surprised if China offered a flat (zero) premium," said a trader. "The current LME prices mean more than enough profits for Chinese smelters. If they use domestic ore, I would think their production costs would be $600 to $700 (a tonne)."
Premiums for spot trade differed widely, with some traders saying they saw offers as low as $20 per tonne and others noting deals with a premium of $85.
"We've seen offers as low as $20 to $30. But we're not sure if they are really going to deliver the metal for that price," said one zinc trader.
The physical copper market remained very quiet following heavy GSP imports last month, traders said. Nominal premiums for the metal were seen unchanged at $60/$70 per tonne.
